jB7jxmY4KEc.speaker: adnan

jB7jxmY4KEc.title: Advancing Towards the Basics: Priorities
jB7jxmY4KEc.one_line: The series opener: Muslims progress by returning to the fundamentals, ranking priorities as the Prophet taught, and the youth must lead it.
jB7jxmY4KEc.summary: With bombing in Gaza resumed, the sheikh says the world tolerates it because the victims are Muslim, and that Canada is complicit. He urges Muslims, a sizeable share of the country and the city, to vote on principle, since citizens whose values never shape policy are hardly citizens. Then he launches the series: everything else progresses by moving on, but Islam progresses by advancing back to the basics. The Prophet taught his companions how to rank what matters, and that list has been lost. Al-Bayyinah says the People of the Book divided only after clear evidence came, though they were asked for little beyond sincere worship. His parable is an employee who argues over the exact shade of the encouraged navy suit while being untrustworthy, late and rude: any company would fire him, yet religious communities promote such people. Shaytan pulls people into minor controversies and ties their ego to them until small communities split. Two billion Muslims agree on Allah's oneness, purpose, death, resurrection and accountability, yet their voice counts for nothing. In the second khutbah he pleads with the young to take life seriously and stick to the basics, citing Abu Bakr's first day and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh converting his tribe.

outline.heading: Opening
Tolerated because the victims are Muslim
outline.gist: Children are pulled from the rubble daily while the world argues about trivia. If the people of Gaza looked different or had other names this would not be allowed, and the country we are proud citizens of is complicit.

outline.heading: Vote on principle, informed
outline.gist: Muslims are a real share of the country and the city. Candidates who took no principled stand on the Holy Land should feel it at the ballot, and the Hikma, NCCM and CMAC guides show who stood for justice.

outline.heading: Or else we are not really citizens
outline.gist: If our values never reach internal or external policy, we are here only to eat, reproduce and own property. Change will take time, organization and money; voting is the simplest start.

outline.heading: Vote by your priorities
outline.gist: Vote on Palestine and what matters to you, not the economy. That is the theme of the series: in this era Muslims are obligated to advance towards the fundamentals of the deen.

outline.heading: Islam progresses back to its basics
outline.gist: Everything else progresses away from what it left behind; Islam advances by understanding and practising the basics the Prophet left. We have lost our way in controversies and tertiary matters.

outline.heading: Fighting over weightless issues
outline.gist: The ummah struggles because it spends its energy dividing over issues of almost no weight while ignoring the vast common ground every Muslim shares.

outline.heading: In pursuit of shabab
outline.gist: He is betting everything on the young people in the room to educate and commit themselves, and is still searching for shabab who care about the ummah rather than their own glory and careers.

outline.heading: Seeing one ummah, as the Prophet did
outline.gist: The Prophet saw his ummah, not nations, races or demographics. We need a generation that feels it belongs to that ummah and carries its burdens, however divided it is.

outline.heading: The Prophet taught priorities
outline.gist: He taught his companions what mattered most, how to rank things and what to set aside in a given situation; over the centuries that priority list was lost.

outline.heading: Divided after the clear proof
outline.gist: Al-Bayyinah: the People of the Book would not change until the clear proof came, a messenger reciting purified pages, and then they divided, though all they were asked was to worship Allah sincerely (98:1-5).

outline.heading: The employee and the navy blue suit
outline.gist: A company values service, teamwork, trust, kindness and punctuality, and merely encourages a navy suit and fresh haircut. An employee who argues over the exact shade of navy while being late, rude and untrustworthy would be fired within a week, never made the one who teaches the company's culture.

outline.heading: What we can leave for a hundred years
outline.gist: Every way of life has priorities. There are many things we can afford not to discuss for a century because the basics demand all our effort; this is the difference between us and the companions.

outline.heading: Pick a scholar and move on
outline.gist: Know what ranks first and what does not rank at all. Choose a scholar you trust on minor matters and let others do the same; in masjids since he was five, he has watched newcomers get lost in details that ruin their mindset.

outline.heading: Shaytan invests your ego in controversy
outline.gist: He has watched small communities split because people tied their ego to a controversy. Shaytan makes it about beating the other person, so no one will lower his wing for the believers (15:88) or take a blow to his pride to keep people together.

outline.heading: Two billion and voiceless
outline.gist: A quarter of humanity agrees on ten or fifteen beliefs whatever their background or madhhab, and still their voice adds up to nothing.

outline.heading: What even two enemies agree on
outline.gist: Sit two Muslims who despise each other down and they agree on Allah's oneness, a purpose to life, death, resurrection, accountability, Paradise and Hell, and the legacy of Muhammad.

outline.heading: How dare you divide His ummah?
outline.gist: They were told to do only a few things, so where does the division come from? You will answer to Allah for dividing His ummah while people were being murdered. We must advance to the basics and stand firm there.

outline.heading: Interlude
What more must happen for the youth to wake?
outline.gist: He asks the young to put down the iPad and the Xbox, learn who they are and what their lives are for, and look at the suffering of people who share their names.

outline.heading: Committed youth make an unstoppable ummah
outline.gist: It is natural for people of forty to sixty to take life seriously; it is rare at fifteen or twenty. An ummah whose youth question their elders' commitment, time and wealth will soon stand on its feet.

outline.heading: The companions were young
outline.gist: The companions who built Islam were in their teens. You do not need to be a scholar or know the whole Quran to carry the concern of the ummah, only something in your heart.

outline.heading: The basics, and nothing more
outline.gist: Know Allah and remove shirk, keep the basic rituals, live the basic ethics of justice, modesty, honesty and trustworthiness that your inner compass already knows, honour your parents, strive for Allah and avoid what you know is harmful.

outline.heading: I didn't live with them, but I lived like them
outline.gist: Look after your inner health and give your life a purpose bigger than yourself, such as the unity of the ummah, so you can tell the Prophet you lived like his companions and perhaps stand beside them.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr's first day
outline.gist: On the day he accepted Islam Abu Bakr returned within hours with some of the greatest companions, knowing less than you know now. It was belonging, identity and passion, not knowledge.

outline.heading: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and his tribe
outline.gist: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, young and respected for his ethics, told his tribe he would not speak to them until they accepted Islam, and they all did in one day.

outline.heading: This ummah was built on people like you
outline.gist: Do not say you are only twelve or seventeen. Change something in your heart, advance to the basics, and you will see change in your life, your surroundings and the ummah.

outline.heading: Ignite the youth, ignite hope
outline.gist: A community finds hope only by inspiring its young to love the deen, the Quran, the Prophet and the ummah. Passion is hard to kindle at forty, but in a fifteen-year-old it is contagious.

outline.heading: Outro

jZvSlMyTS4w.title: Tafsir of Surat Al-Saffat, Part 9: Verses 171-182
jZvSlMyTS4w.one_line: The closing verses of Saffat: Allah's promise of victory to His obedient soldiers, the end of oppressors, and Ramadan as a launching pad.
jZvSlMyTS4w.summary: He reads the end of Saffat as a farewell to Ramadan in uncertain times. Allah's word has long reached the messengers: they and His soldiers will prevail. He explains that a jundi is anyone who takes orders from Allah and, like a soldier, does not demand reasons first, which ties back to the surah's theme of submission. Twice the Prophet is told to turn away from his opponents for a while and watch, because every oppressor ends in loss. He illustrates with Abu Sufyan before the conquest of Makkah: his lie in Madinah, Abbas protecting him, the words of Yusuf's brothers he was coached to say, the army parading past him, and the Prophet giving him a face-saving honour once he was broken. What matters is how things end, and knowing the end is why the Prophet could forgive. Worry about whether you are among the soldiers, not about the oppressors. He explains Lord of Might as the unfathomable, then turns to Ramadan: Allah places our happiest moments inside deprivation. Current suffering is a painful stimulus to wake a living ummah, which is measured by conscience, not numbers. He urges people to use Ramadan to change their trajectory and to live for something larger than themselves.

outline.heading: Opening
The surah's ending as a summary for uncertain times
outline.gist: Muslims in the West and elsewhere live with fear about the future; the end of a surah about submission speaks directly to that.

outline.heading: Interlude
Our word has long reached Our messengers
outline.gist: Kalimah in Arabic means a meaningful statement or decree, not a single word; here it is Allah's standing decree.

outline.heading: The decree: the messengers will be helped and prevail
outline.gist: Allah's aid and final victory belong to His messengers and those who stand for Him.

outline.heading: Allah's soldiers do not question commands
outline.gist: A jundi is anyone who takes orders from Allah; unlike a physician who must question a supervisor, a soldier obeys first, and so do we with Allah.

outline.heading: The suffering of Muslims who are no different from you
outline.gist: Only Allah's choice of where you were born separates you from those suffering now; His decree of victory still stands.

outline.heading: Turn away from them for a while and watch
outline.gist: The Prophet is told twice to leave his opponents for a time and observe the outcome.

outline.heading: Every oppressor ends in loss
outline.gist: Tyrants are punished in themselves, their families or their legacy, yet humanity keeps repeating tyranny.

outline.heading: The Prophet's grief for his opponents
outline.gist: He wept for them because he could see how pitiful they would be once stripped of power.

outline.heading: Are they hastening Our punishment?
outline.gist: When punishment descends on their courtyard, it is an evil morning for those who were warned.

outline.heading: The second command: watch in general
outline.gist: The first command concerns Quraysh specifically; the second covers all oppressors.

outline.heading: Abu Sufyan's lie in Madinah and Umar's anger
outline.gist: Abu Sufyan lied about the broken treaty; when Abbas brought him toward the Prophet, Umar wanted his head.

outline.heading: Abbas calms Umar
outline.gist: Umar answers that he rejoiced more at Abbas's Islam than he would have at his own father's, because it pleased the Prophet.

outline.heading: The words of Yusuf's brothers
outline.gist: Ali advised Abu Sufyan to say what Yusuf's brothers said, knowing the Prophet would answer with Yusuf's reply.

outline.heading: The Prophet's forgiveness and the call to Islam
outline.gist: Abu Sufyan, overwhelmed by the Prophet's patience and generosity, has no answer left.

outline.heading: Abu Sufyan watches the army pass
outline.gist: Standing on a hill he sees tribe after tribe in Islam and the Prophet's disciplined battalion, and calls it kingship; Abbas answers that it is prophethood.

outline.heading: Safety in Abu Sufyan's house: honour for a broken man
outline.gist: The redundant grant of safety was given to restore some dignity to a man left with nothing.

outline.heading: It is all about how it ends
outline.gist: Do not be fooled by strong beginnings; knowing the ending is what made the Prophet merciful.

outline.heading: Forgive my people, for they do not know
outline.gist: Wounded at Uhud he prayed for them; worry about whether you are among Allah's soldiers, not about the oppressor.

outline.heading: Lord of Might: the unfathomable
outline.gist: Izzah carries both dignity and being beyond comprehension; you will not see the wisdom in everything, and that is acceptable.

outline.heading: Peace upon the messengers and praise to the Lord of the worlds
outline.gist: How would anyone have this guidance without the prophets who brought it?

outline.heading: The bittersweet end of Ramadan
outline.gist: Ramadan never grows old; it shows a potential within us we keep refusing to reach.

outline.heading: The paradox: happiest in the middle of deprivation
outline.gist: Without food, drink or sleep, people are happier than on any vacation, and weep when it leaves.

outline.heading: Current suffering as a sternal rub for the ummah
outline.gist: Like the painful test of whether a patient is alive, these trials are meant to wake the ummah.

outline.heading: The ummah is alive: not a matter of numbers
outline.gist: Life is measured in conscience, empathy and willingness to sacrifice, not headcount.

outline.heading: Living for something bigger than yourself
outline.gist: The feeling of Ramadan nights can stay with you if you live as His soldier; communal night prayer was organized so others could taste it.

outline.heading: Allah will make you answer: how dedicated are you?
outline.gist: Everyone will face moments that establish whether their commitment is full or partial.

outline.heading: Praise of Allah amid loss in Gaza
outline.gist: People praying in the open beside destroyed mosques and completing the Quran show what is truly valuable, without excusing our inaction.

outline.heading: Ramadan as a launching pad and yearly boot camp
outline.gist: Use it to change your trajectory; the ummah rises when individuals improve inside and cooperate outside.

outline.heading: Outro

Jo3FS675r_0.title: Approaching the Election: What We Know
Jo3FS675r_0.one_line: Five certainties every Muslim must accept, from owning our fate to unity, as common ground for planning ahead of the federal election.
Jo3FS675r_0.summary: On the busiest Friday of the year, with schoolchildren and students present, the sheikh opens with 39:9 and argues that any sound plan must be built on certainty, not likelihood, citing the legal maxim that certainty is not removed by doubt. He offers five certainties that everyone must accept, even those who dislike him, as common ground. First, the ummah's fate is in its own hands: the Prophet asked that no outside enemy be given power over it, and 24:55 ties succession on earth to faith and righteous deeds, so failure is ours and blaming conspirators is the easy way out. Second, this is not the ummah's worst moment: Ibn al-Athir wrote of the Tatars as the obituary of Islam, and the Black Stone was held for 22 years from 317 AH, yet the ummah rose again; recovery is possible, not promised. Third, the deen was built by the young, from Ali and Zayd to the youths of the Cave, and students who pushed universities to divest have already proven it. Fourth, each person is charged with his full capacity, and voting by Gaza is the smallest part of it. Fifth, strength lies in unity, and he asks whether people are not tired of division.

outline.heading: Opening
Plans must rest on certainty
outline.gist: Opening with 39:9 and the presence of students, he says the point is not seeking knowledge but planning: a plan built on likelihoods fails, certainty is not removed by doubt, and the Prophet said to leave what makes you doubt.

outline.heading: Five certainties as common ground
outline.gist: Even those who dislike him must accept these five, because they are not his; agreed certainties give the community common ground to move forward.

outline.heading: Certainty one: our fate is in our hands
outline.gist: The Prophet asked that no outside enemy be given power to destroy his ummah and it was granted, and 24:55 makes succession conditional; if we are not in charge on earth, we have not met the condition.

outline.heading: Blaming conspirators is the easy way out
outline.gist: Pointing a finger spares us self-criticism and change; Allah took that excuse away, and he counts it a blessing that no one else controls our fate.

outline.heading: Certainty two: this is not our worst time
outline.gist: Many feel we have hit bottom, but the ummah has been through far worse and came out holding to its identity, language, deen and sacred places.

outline.heading: Ibn al-Athir and the Tatars
outline.gist: In al-Kamil, Ibn al-Athir avoided writing of the Tatar invasion for years, calling it the obituary of Islam and wishing he had never been born.

outline.heading: Recovery is possible, not promised
outline.gist: The ummah rose, found its heart and renewed its glory after that; he does not promise it will happen again, only that it is possible and the choice is ours.

outline.heading: 317 AH: the Black Stone taken for 22 years
outline.gist: Look up the year 317: the Qarmatians took the Black Stone from the Kaaba and kept it for 22 years, a lower point than today, and historians called it the end of Islam.

outline.heading: We have come back before
outline.gist: He does not sell illusions; having recovered from lower points, the ummah has proven it can do it again.

outline.heading: Certainty three: the deen was built by the young
outline.gist: The first people the Prophet called were Ali at about ten and Zayd; the companions who built the deen, men and women, were young.

outline.heading: Thirty years to three continents
outline.gist: An ummah that does not guide, embrace and empower its youth has no future; within thirty years of his death Islam spanned three continents because he raised young people to carry it.

outline.heading: The youths of the Cave
outline.gist: Muslims read Al-Kahf every Friday yet overlook its lesson: a handful of believing youths under twenty changed their nation's history.

outline.heading: The ages of the companions
outline.gist: In English he goes over how young Ali, Zubayr, Talhah, Sa'd, Sa'id, Fatimah, Aisha and Asma were when they carried the message.

outline.heading: Invest in who stands here fifty years from now
outline.gist: Fifty years on we will be forgotten; a masjid stays alive only if we invest today in the young people who will stand in it.

outline.heading: Students already moved universities to divest
outline.gist: His generation was broken politically, but students in encampments, MSAs and schools made universities divest and proved they can shift the needle.

outline.heading: Allah sees the young as the future
outline.gist: Institutions may not invest in them, but Allah sees them as the solution; their passion and idealism matter, and the future leaders are sitting among us.

outline.heading: Interlude
Certainty four: you owe your full capacity
outline.gist: Each person answers for himself; Allah charges only what you can bear, but all of it, not half or three quarters.

outline.heading: Listen to those who know, then vote
outline.gist: Give what you have in money, effort, pen, tongue or advocacy. Voting costs almost nothing; he knows nothing of Canadian politics, having grown up where the word was dangerous, so listen to those who know.

outline.heading: Vote by Gaza, not the economy
outline.gist: Others vote on the economy; vote by who stood with truth, so politicians who ignored the blood of children taste political loss. Muslims can swing any election.

outline.heading: Be the voice of those under the rubble
outline.gist: Voting is a small thing, not the whole duty, but through it you can make heard those killed under their homes.

outline.heading: Make them feel the sting
outline.gist: Listen to informed advocates and vote on principle: after seventeen months of children killed in real time, politicians without integrity must feel the cost, and you should make clear why you voted.

outline.heading: We share the blame if we stay home
outline.gist: Unprincipled politicians stay in office partly because Muslims do not exercise their right; let the child never pulled from the rubble be heard in your vote.

outline.heading: Certainty five: strength is in unity
outline.gist: The ummah's strength is in mutual support, love and mercy; work to gather it and never add to its division.

outline.heading: Are you not tired of division?
outline.gist: How many more must die before we drop our pride and gather people as the Prophet did? He asks if people are not sick of empty debates and Muslims pitted against each other.

outline.heading: Every Muslim agrees on these five
outline.gist: Any Muslim anywhere, practising or not, agrees with these five, so there is common ground; begin from what we know and work it out as we go.

outline.heading: Outro

ELPud0MamCU.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 29: Tahajjud
ELPud0MamCU.one_line: Two reminders: a severed finger shows what the body is worth and what disciplined worship buys, then tribulations from Pakistan to Gaza and believers as one building.
ELPud0MamCU.summary: The twenty-ninth night has two reminders between the rakaat. The first rests on one story: a fit friend who keeps a strict exercise routine slips from a chin-up bar in the United States and severs a finger. The speaker asks the congregation what they would pay to have it reattached, has them make a fist without one finger, and then reveals that the care cost close to a quarter of a million dollars and the finger still never felt normal. If one finger is worth that, what would you pay to rescue your whole body? That price cannot be paid in money, he says, but those standing in prayer on this last night are paying it, and only discipline, in sport, in excellent work or in worship, brings a certain clarity. Do not be the one who says he wishes he had sent ahead for his life. The second reminder begins with how hard it is to watch Gaza in real time. The speaker recalls relief work after the 2005 Pakistan earthquake, lists a generation of tribulations from Bosnia through Iraq, Libya and Syria to Gaza, and closes with the hadith of believers as a building: each person is a brick holding up the others and must build his own physical, mental and spiritual strength.

outline.heading: Interlude
A friend's fitness routine and a severed finger
outline.gist: A friend who guards his health and keeps a strict workout routine even on trips slips from a chin-up bar while doing CrossFit in the United States and loses a finger, which he carries to hospital on ice.

outline.heading: What would you pay for one finger?
outline.gist: He asks the audience to name a price for reattaching it, explains how complex the hand is, and has everyone make a fist without one finger to feel how much strength it holds.

outline.heading: A quarter-million-dollar finger that never feels the same
outline.gist: The care cost nearly a quarter of a million US dollars, and even after microsurgery the finger stays stiff and never feels normal, yet the man was glad to pay.

outline.heading: Paying for the whole body tonight through disciplined worship
outline.gist: If a finger is worth that much, what would you pay to rescue your whole body? No money can buy it, but standing in prayer on this last night is that payment; a certain clarity comes only through discipline, whether in sport, work or worship.

outline.heading: If only I had sent ahead for my life
outline.gist: Everyone standing tonight and seeking forgiveness is doing what the regretful soul on the Day of Judgment wishes it had done; the month of training is meant to spare you that regret.

outline.heading: Interlude
How hard it is to watch Gaza in real time
outline.gist: He acknowledges the pain of watching the conflict live: around two million people driven from their homes, tens of thousands killed, wealth destroyed and some 150,000 injured, with the true figures likely higher.

outline.heading: The 2005 Pakistan earthquake: a double catastrophe
outline.gist: Tens of thousands died in seconds in a beautiful mountain region; concrete homes fell on the women who were inside while the men worked outdoors, leaving men alone with children, a social catastrophe on top of the physical one.

outline.heading: Relief work in the ruined villages
outline.gist: As a young graduate he went with friends to help and wondered how anyone in those devastated villages of simple farmers wrapped in blankets could ever be happy again.

outline.heading: A show of hands for a son who returns to serve
outline.gist: When a visitor asked the village men whether they would be glad if one of their sons were educated in America and came back to serve them, every hand went up in joy, a sign of hope that survives ruin.

outline.heading: A generation of tribulations: Bosnia, Iraq, Libya, Syria, Gaza
outline.gist: He traces one catastrophe after another: the camps and killings in Bosnia, the two Iraq wars, Libya and Syria with its million dead, and now Gaza, as tests Allah places on this ummah.

outline.heading: Believers as a building: each brick holds up the others
outline.gist: Like bricks in a wall, every believer carries those beside him, so each must build his own physical, mental and spiritual strength, accept Allah's decree and be willing to sacrifice.

Xse5Aniugf4.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 29: Endings and Beginnings
Xse5Aniugf4.one_line: Every ending precedes a beginning: the soul at peace returning to its Lord, giving to seek His Face, and the weighing of deeds.
Xse5Aniugf4.summary: On the last night of Ramadan he frames the Quran as constantly describing transitions: people change gradually, life moves from childhood to old age, plants grow and wither, someone dies as someone is born, and for the Infinite every death is only a passage to a new beginning. Seeing life this way should lead us to leave a good start for those who come after, even if our own start was hard. From Al-Fajr 89:23-30 he contrasts the person who remembers too late and wishes he had sent something ahead with the soul at peace, purified through a lifetime of tazkiyah, which is called back to its Lord, admitted first among His servants and then into His Garden. From Al-Layl 92:14-21 he explains taqwa as pausing to ask whether an act displeases Allah, and giving wealth to purify oneself rather than to repay anyone, illustrated by the Prophet repaying every favour except Abu Bakr's and the story of Abu Bakr giving away his caravan. From Al-Qari'ah 101:6-11 he says the social rankings of this world vanish and only the weight of one's scales counts. He closes with hadith on weightless deeds and the card bearing Allah's name that outweighs ninety-nine scrolls, urging people to fill their scales tonight.

outline.heading: Opening
You get paid at the end of the job
outline.gist: Many scholars hold that the greatest reward comes on the final night, since a worker is paid when the job is done.

outline.heading: Interlude
The Quran speaks constantly of transitions
outline.gist: A person who commits to change transforms gradually, often without noticing, the way we only see ageing in old photos.

outline.heading: For the Infinite, every death is a transition
outline.gist: Time does not bind Allah, so for His creation any ending is the moment before the next beginning: Ramadan ends and Eid begins.

outline.heading: The cycle of endings and beginnings
outline.gist: Life passes through stages, plants grow green then yellow and return with rain, and at every moment someone dies while someone is born, which humbles us.

outline.heading: Give someone else a good beginning
outline.gist: If your own start was hard, make up for it by ensuring those who come after you begin well.

outline.heading: Bidding Ramadan farewell
outline.gist: We do not know whether we will live another Ramadan; all we need is for Allah to accept us once.

outline.heading: Interlude
Jahannam brought forth and remembrance too late
outline.gist: On that day the human finally reflects deeply, but the reflection brings no benefit.

outline.heading: I wish I had sent ahead for my life
outline.gist: The true life is the next one; status, investments and effort were all left behind, and no punishment is like His.

outline.heading: The soul at peace
outline.gist: The tranquil soul is one its owner purified through tazkiyah, transforming its desires until it found Allah's love.

outline.heading: Others run like scattered locusts
outline.gist: The rest leave their graves in fear, running aimlessly, not knowing what they flee or where to.

outline.heading: Every road ends at Allah
outline.gist: However people turn and scheme, every path ends at the foot of His throne; those who prepared for this are calm.

outline.heading: Return to your Lord, pleased and pleasing
outline.gist: It is a return to where you came from; the soul comes back content and its Lord content with it.

outline.heading: Servanthood as dignity
outline.gist: Allah's highest compliment is calling someone His servant, as He does the Prophet; seeing yourself as His servant is a source of dignity and freedom.

outline.heading: First the company of servants, then the Garden
outline.gist: Entering among His servants and entering His paradise are two steps: first admission to the group whose only concern was serving Allah well, then the place.

outline.heading: A beginning that requires an ending
outline.gist: Paradise is a beginning we cannot fully comprehend, granted only after accepting the end that precedes it.

outline.heading: Warning of a blazing fire for the most wretched
outline.gist: No one enters it by conscious choice; those who made the worst choices, denied the message and turned away bring misery on themselves.

outline.heading: Taqwa as asking first: will this displease Allah?
outline.gist: The one kept from the fire is the most mindful; even when he asks and still slips, the question shows Allah was present in his heart.

outline.heading: Giving wealth to be purified
outline.gist: The giving is done seeking purity of soul and wealth; zakat is someone else's right, and keeping it means eating what is theirs.

outline.heading: The Prophet repaid every favour
outline.gist: He kept track of every kindness done to him and returned it, so he would owe no one and keep his reward whole.

outline.heading: Here is my back: settling accounts before death
outline.gist: Before he died he invited anyone he had struck or whose wealth he had taken to claim it from him, and some did.

outline.heading: Except Abu Bakr, whom only Allah can repay
outline.gist: He said he had repaid everyone's kindness except Abu Bakr's, left it to Allah, and ordered every door into the masjid closed except Abu Bakr's.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr gives away his caravan
outline.gist: In a time of hunger he gave away a whole caravan, its camels, his household goods and finally his garment.

outline.heading: Wearing a sack: his Lord is pleased with him
outline.gist: Summoned to the masjid in a sack, he was told Allah asks whether he is pleased with his Lord, for his Lord is pleased with him; he gave seeking only His Face.

outline.heading: Al-Qari'ah: a blow that changes the essence
outline.gist: The qari'ah is a strike so hard it transforms what it hits; everything about that day is unfamiliar.

outline.heading: The social laws that rank us will change
outline.gist: Lineage, wealth, credentials, looks and age decide our standing here, and children learn the ranking early; those laws will not apply.

outline.heading: The nobleman and the poor man
outline.gist: The Prophet said the dishevelled man people would ignore is worth more than an earthful of the nobleman.

outline.heading: Pursue status, but know it is not who you are
outline.gist: Titles and signatures help you influence change in this world, but you arrive with none of them, and no one will stand for you there.

outline.heading: Only the weight of your scales
outline.gist: Presidents, generals and CEOs are ranked only by the weight of their deeds; you come with just your name and your parent's name.

outline.heading: The left scale fills anyway
outline.gist: We all sin, so concentrate on filling the right scale; a night like this can outweigh a lifetime.

outline.heading: A pleasing life
outline.gist: The one with heavy scales lives a life he is content with overall.

outline.heading: The big man who weighs nothing
outline.gist: A huge man throws himself on the scale in desperation but weighs less than a mosquito's wing.

outline.heading: Mountains of deeds that float
outline.gist: Some come with deeds like mountains that become weightless; the companions were told these people pray at night like them.

outline.heading: Violating Allah's limits when alone
outline.gist: They disobey whenever only Allah is watching, without shame before Him, so their deeds are hollowed out from inside.

outline.heading: His mother is a bottomless pit
outline.gist: The mother is the place one turns to for care; for this person the kindest refuge is a blazing abyss.

outline.heading: Interlude
The card that outweighed ninety-nine scrolls
outline.gist: A man faces ninety-nine scrolls of sins and admits them all, but is called back for one card bearing the testimony of faith, which outweighs everything, for no one is wronged that day.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire
themes.note: The calm soul's return, the warning of the blazing fire and the weighing of deeds frame the night.

themes.label: Mortality, death and preparing for it
themes.note: Death is a transition, not an end; every ending is the moment before a new beginning, which should make us prepare and leave something for those who follow.

themes.label: Tazkiyah: purifying and training the self
themes.note: The soul at peace is one its owner purified over a lifetime until it found Allah's love.

themes.label: Taqwa and God-consciousness
themes.note: Taqwa is asking before every word or act whether it would displease Allah, which keeps Him present in the heart.

themes.label: Zakat, charity and giving
themes.note: Giving is meant to purify the soul and wealth and to seek Allah's Face, not to repay favours; zakat withheld is someone else's right consumed.

themes.label: The companions and the early generations
themes.note: Abu Bakr's total generosity and the Prophet's inability to repay him illustrate giving for Allah alone.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: Wealth, titles and status mean nothing on the Day of Judgment; only the weight of one's deeds counts.

themes.label: Sins, their causes and remedies
themes.note: Those who violate Allah's limits whenever they are alone find their mountains of deeds weightless.

themes.label: Tawhid and worship of Allah alone
themes.note: The testimony of faith outweighs ninety-nine scrolls of sins.

quran.point: Rain brings out green plants that later turn yellow and crumble: the visible cycle of beginnings and endings.
People leave their graves with downcast eyes like scattered locusts, calling it a difficult day.

hadith.gist: Before his death the Prophet told people that anyone he had struck could take retribution from his back and anyone whose wealth he had taken could take it back.
No one did the Prophet a favour except that he repaid it, except Abu Bakr, whose favour Allah will repay; every door into the masjid was to be closed except Abu Bakr's.
Jibril told the Prophet to ask Abu Bakr, dressed in a sack after giving everything away, whether he was pleased with his Lord, for his Lord was pleased with him.
A poor man people would ignore is better than an earthful of the nobleman they honour.
A huge, fat man will come on the Day of Resurrection and weigh less than the wing of a mosquito.
People will come with deeds like mountains that Allah makes scattered dust; they pray at night like you, but when alone with Allah's prohibitions they violate them.
A man with ninety-nine scrolls of sins is saved by a single card bearing the testimony of faith, which outweighs them all.

maxims: Every ending is the moment before a new beginning
You don't get paid halfway; you get paid at the end
Make up for a bad beginning by giving someone a good one
It's a return: you are going back
Your VIP card will not open any gates there
Before you act, ask: will this displease Allah?

stories.who: The Prophet's farewell to his community
stories.point: He settled every possible debt and harm before death so he would owe no one.

stories.who: Abu Bakr gives away his caravan and his clothes
stories.point: Giving purely for Allah's Face, not to repay anyone, earns Allah's pleasure; the story's chain is debated but its lesson is sound.

stories.who: The nobleman and the dishevelled man passing the Prophet
stories.point: Worldly status is not Allah's measure.

stories.who: The man with ninety-nine scrolls and one card
stories.point: No one is wronged that day, and Allah's name outweighs everything.

contemporary: Social ranking by credentials, titles, wealth and lineage
takeaways: See every ending, including the end of Ramadan, as the start of something new and prepare for what follows.
Work to leave those who come after you a better beginning than you had.
Before speaking or acting, ask whether it would displease Allah.
Give your wealth seeking purity and Allah's Face, and pay the zakat that belongs to others.
Guard your conduct when no one but Allah is watching, and fill your right-hand scale on nights like these.

2:67.en: And when Moses said unto his people: Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye sacrifice a cow, they said: Dost thou make game of us? He answered: Allah forbid that I should be among the foolish

2:68.ar: قَالُواْ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا هِيَۚ قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ يَقُولُ إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةࣱ لَّا فَارِضࣱ وَلَا بِكۡرٌ عَوَانُۢ بَيۡنَ ذَٰلِكَۖ فَٱفۡعَلُواْ مَا تُؤۡمَرُونَ

2:69.ar: قَالُواْ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا لَوۡنُهَاۚ قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ يَقُولُ إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةࣱ صَفۡرَآءُ فَاقِعࣱ لَّوۡنُهَا تَسُرُّ ٱلنَّٰظِرِينَ

2:71.en: (Moses) answered: Lo! He saith: Verily she is a cow unyoked; she plougheth not the soil nor watereth the tilth; whole and without mark. They said: Now thou bringest the truth. So they sacrificed her, though almost they did not

20krVqmJABI.speaker_note: Speaks as the imam about his masjid's Ramadan volunteers and Eid-night prayer, and refers to his year-long theme of returning to the basics.
20krVqmJABI.title: Continuing After Ramadan
20krVqmJABI.one_line: A week after Ramadan, keep part of what you built through small consistent deeds, stick to the basics, and choose one avenue of service.
20krVqmJABI.summary: One week after Eid, the sheikh says sliding back into old habits is normal and the contrast with Ramadan is meant to be felt, not to bring despair. Masjids are fine during Eid week but start to weep now, and the 90 Ramadan volunteers shrink to a fraction, though the Lord of Ramadan is the Lord of every month. Building on 64:16, fear Allah as much as you are able, he says no one can keep Ramadan's pace, and the Prophet even forbade fasting every day. What matters is keeping something, as the most beloved deeds are those done consistently. He ties this to his year-long theme of returning to the basics: everyone has an opinion on moon sighting while few could pass a quiz on who Allah is. The Israelites ruined themselves with questions about the cow, and Shaytan's trick is to absorb you in weightless religious debates you will not question. Islam is simple; leave the details to scholars and your local imam. He gives seven steps: two pages of Quran daily, daily dhikr, one congregational prayer kept, some witr, daily dua, one of five avenues of service (education, mentorship, outreach, finances, advocacy), and something for your own growth. Advocacy and voting are the minimum, and the masjid must become the community's shared home.

outline.heading: Opening
Fear Allah as much as you are able
outline.gist: 64:16 asks for mindfulness, listening, obedience and spending to the best of one's ability; a week after Ramadan, sliding back into old habits is normal and expected.

outline.heading: The contrast is meant to be felt
outline.gist: Seeing what was lost since the night the Quran was completed is not a reason for self-loathing or despair; it shows the difference so you decide what to retain. Empty masjids on the first days of Eid are normal.

outline.heading: Masjids start weeping now
outline.gist: After Eid week masjids wonder where people went, Fajr and Isha empty again, and 90 Ramadan volunteers shrink to a fraction, yet the Lord of Ramadan is the Lord of Shawwal and every other month.

outline.heading: A taste of what awaits, then it is taken
outline.gist: Allah gave a taste of closeness no one could reach alone, then Shaytan returned to your heart; you only know sugar by salt and relief by pain, so the question is which state you want.

outline.heading: You are not asked to copy Ramadan
outline.gist: Do what you are able to; keeping Ramadan's pace is impossible, and the Prophet forbade fasting every day: fast some days and break others.

outline.heading: Not cold turkey: the consistent deed
outline.gist: Take on the deeds you can sustain, since Allah does not tire until you do; the deed He loved most was the one done consistently, even if small.

outline.heading: Avoid the haram, do what you can of the commands
outline.gist: Abu Salamah would recite the verse on those constant in their prayer when narrating the hadith on consistent deeds; the Prophet said to avoid what he forbade completely and do what you can of what he commanded, since earlier nations were ruined by their questions.

outline.heading: Back to the basics
outline.gist: His theme for the past year: we waste time arguing details that lifelong scholars cannot agree on, and everyone has an opinion on moon sighting.

outline.heading: Why carry accountability no one asked of you?
outline.gist: Few could pass a quiz on who Allah is and what is expected of them ethically; leave the details to scholars, follow your local imam, and you are not accountable for them.

outline.heading: The cow: questions that ruined a people
outline.gist: No sane person asks for more to defend before Allah, yet the Israelites argued over the cow's colour, size, spots and lineage and made a simple command hard.

outline.heading: A lifetime is not enough for the basics
outline.gist: Basic ethics, compassion, humility, integrity and modesty take a lifetime to learn, while people pursue questions earlier scholars would not even ask.

outline.heading: Shaytan's trick: obsession inside the deen
outline.gist: Pushed outside the deen you would notice, so Shaytan absorbs you in weightless debates inside it that change nothing in your character, and you never question yourself because it feels religious.

outline.heading: Islam is simple; we made it complex
outline.gist: Ramadan's beauty was simple: pray behind an imam and stop eating and drinking. Allah wants ease for you; like those who complicated the cow, we made the deen complex.

outline.heading: We cannot afford the details
outline.gist: We barely have time to learn the Prophet's ethics and how he lived; weighing evidence on details takes years of study, Arabic, legal history and command of the whole Quran and hadith.

outline.heading: Step one: two pages of Quran a day
outline.gist: An ummah that agrees on 99% divides itself over details; instead open the Quran from the start and read two pages a day to finish by next Ramadan, since nothing else fills the gap between you and Allah.

outline.heading: Step two: daily dhikr
outline.gist: Keep a fixed, counted daily remembrance, because work, family, the gym and friends can take 12 to 14 hours without a single thought of God.

outline.heading: One congregational prayer and nightly witr
outline.gist: Step three: bring back at least one of the congregational prayers kept in Ramadan, such as Fajr or Isha, to fix your routine. Step four: keep even three rakahs of witr every night.

outline.heading: Step five: keep speaking to Allah
outline.gist: Do not switch off the daily dua of Ramadan; these five basics are a baseline, and anyone who has them should add one small step.

outline.heading: The Eid-night prayer felt different
outline.gist: The night prayer after Ramadan, half as long, still felt too long and half the people left, because what was there has been taken away; give it time to return.

outline.heading: Interlude
Step six: commit to one of five avenues
outline.gist: Muslims in the West should each choose one avenue, education, mentorship, outreach, financial centralization or advocacy, and not try to do everything.

outline.heading: Especially advocacy
outline.gist: Choose what you are good at, but if nothing else, advocate: the beheaded children of Gaza should keep asking you how this is still happening.

outline.heading: Vote by principle, not the economy
outline.gist: Push back even with a small force: vote in the coming weeks after reading what Muslim advocacy groups publish, so officials feel the sting of ignoring principle.

outline.heading: Everyone will be asked about advocacy
outline.gist: Voting is the bare minimum; you may not be asked about teaching or dawah, but everyone will be asked about speaking for justice and the voiceless.

outline.heading: Their children are your children
outline.gist: The parent losing his children is a mirror of you; distancing yourself means losing basic empathy, mercy and brotherhood.

outline.heading: Step seven: something in it for you
outline.gist: Everyone must both give and receive, learning and being cared for weekly; someone who only gives will burn out.

outline.heading: Some give just by listening
outline.gist: No one should only take; some give time or expertise, others just listen, since many in the community simply need someone to talk to.

outline.heading: The masjid as the community's umbrella
outline.gist: Stepping out of our silos only to pray gets us nowhere; the Prophet's masjid brought everyone together, though not everyone got along.

outline.heading: A family you do not all like
outline.gist: The companions still stood shoulder to shoulder as family; taking only what you want is an entitled mindset he sees more in the West than anywhere, when life is accepted whole.

outline.heading: Carry Ramadan's fuel into service
outline.gist: Do not go back to how you were; use the spiritual energy of Ramadan to serve the ummah in your own way, so everyone's efforts meet and become something powerful.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: The masjid: its role and etiquette
themes.note: Everyone must both give and receive at the masjid; it should be the umbrella under which the community lives as a family, as the Prophet's masjid was, not a place to step into for prayer and leave.

quran.point: Fear Allah as much as you are able, listen, obey and spend; those saved from their own stinginess succeed.
Those who are constant in their prayer: Abu Salamah recited it whenever he narrated the hadith on consistent deeds.
The Israelites' endless questions about the cow made things hard for themselves.
Allah wants ease for you, not hardship: Islam is simple and we made it complex.

hadith.gist: The Prophet forbade fasting continuously; fast some days and break others.
Take on the deeds you can sustain, for Allah does not tire until you tire; the deed He loved most was the one done consistently, even if small.
What I forbid you, avoid; what I command you, do what you can of it; those before you were destroyed by their many questions and disputes with their prophets.

stories.who: The Israelites and the cow
stories.point: Their questions about colour, size and lineage made a simple command hard; obsessing over details was their downfall.

stories.who: The Prophet's masjid
stories.point: Not everyone got along, but they respected each other and stood shoulder to shoulder as one family.

takeaways: Keep part of your Ramadan routine: two pages of Quran, daily dhikr, one congregational prayer, some witr and daily dua.
Choose small, sustainable deeds over bursts you cannot keep.
Stop arguing details that scholars debate; follow your local imam and focus on the basics.
Pick one avenue of service (education, mentorship, outreach, finances or advocacy), and at minimum advocate and vote by principle.
Make sure you also receive learning and care, and help make the masjid the community's home.
